name: Amazigh (Berber) peoples
subtitle: Amazigh (Berber) peoples: who the sources name, where they live, and what the old labels got wrong.

image.alt: A multi-storey stone fortified granary with small wooden windows and a central courtyard in the Anti-Atlas mountains.
image.caption: The collective fortified granary (agadir) of Inoumar in Morocco's Anti-Atlas, a communal storehouse managed for centuries by Amazigh village assemblies.

parts.text: The Tifinagh alphabet, known as Libyco-Berber, has been used for over 2,500 years; Tamazight languages are described as developing from the Numidian language.

Libyco-Berber (Libyc) inscriptions are found from the Canary Islands to Libya and from the Mediterranean to Niger; over 1,300 are known, mostly funerary; the Tuareg still use a form of the script. Source is a lower-tier journal (WASET).

Speaker numbers by country vary and are contested: estimates of Libya about 600,000 speakers; Tunisia 200,000 to close to 500,000; Morocco as many as half of 35 million 'speak or understand'; Algeria almost a third of 42 million (journalist's figures, 2020).
2011-06/07: Morocco's 2011 constitution recognises Amazigh as an official language; commentary at the time said the status would be implemented slowly. Referendum scheduled 1 July 2011.

2002: Algeria granted Tamazight 'national' language status in 2002, following large-scale rioting in Kabylia. (A 2017 Washington Institute article instead dates the decree to March 2003; sources differ.)

2016-02-07: Algerian parliament passed a constitutional amendment on 7 February 2016 recognising Berber as an official language; Article 4 says Tamazight is national and official, Arabic remaining the official language of the State (Art. 3), with an academy and an organic law to set implementation.
2016: Constitutional text of Algeria's 2016 revision, Article 4.

2020: Equal Times (2020): in Algeria official status is 'only guaranteed in Kabylie' per one account; Libya's Amazigh cities have de facto autonomy without constitutional recognition; Tunisia has seen 'fewer changes'.
1980-03-10: The Berber Spring began on 10 March 1980 with clashes between Algerian security forces and Berber students and activists (known in Tamazight as Tafsut Imaziyen/Imazighen).
Article 6 of the 1930 dahir sent criminal cases in Berber lands to French law; it was rescinded in 1934. Urban outcry did not lead to repeal of the courts.

French officials and scholars treated law as a window into 'Berber psychology' and assumed Berber customary law was distinct from, even hostile to, Islamic law; Hoffman questions the 'divide and rule' account.

The Arab/Berber divide is analysed as tied to the transformation of the Imazighen into a cultural minority by the nation-state and to French colonial constructs such as the Kabyle Myth (abstract only).
The term 'Berber' was revived by French colonialism in the nineteenth century; postcolonial states often treated Berber identity as folklore.

blocks.q: Myth or fact: Common claim: French Berber policy was simply 'divide and rule' that removed Berber areas from Islamic law.
blocks.explain: A peer-reviewed study calls the removal-from-Islamic-law claim 'empirically untenable in several respects' and notes missionaries did little work there.

items.when: c. 3rd century BC to 3rd century AD (antiquity)
items.text: Libyc/Numidian inscriptions: the Libyco-Berber script, ancestor of Tifinagh, appears across the Maghreb, most from the Numidian kingdom. Exact dating of script origin is still unsettled per the author. Only the 1,300 count and Numidian origin of most are sourced from a readable page; the 3rd-century-BC start date came from a search summary of a Wikipedia mirror, not cited.
The conquest lasted about a century and a half; by the 740s Berber opposition stretched 'from Tripolitania to Tangier'.
The 'Berber Dahir' was issued by the Moroccan sultan, designed by Protectorate officials.
Morocco recognises Tamazight as official; Algeria follows in 2016.
